Under Regulation E, federal law protects consumers against unauthorized electronic transfers. But when a scammer posing as your bank, Amazon, or an AI voice of someone you know convinces you to hit send, the transfer is usually considered authorized. Banks rely on that distinction to deny reimbursement.

Consumers lost more than $1 billion this way through Zelle between 2017 and 2023. New York’s Attorney General is now suing Zelle’s operator, Early Warning Services, and a judge has refused to dismiss the case. The CFPB dropped its own version of the lawsuit, leaving most consumers with no federal recourse right now.
